{{Short description|Statistical technique}}
In [[statistics]], '''polychoric correlation'''<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://support.sas.com/documentation/cdl/en/procstat/65543/HTML/default/viewer.htm#procstat_corr_details14.htm|title=Base SAS(R) 9.3 Procedures Guide: Statistical Procedures, Second Edition|website=support.sas.com|language=en|access-date=2018-01-10}}</ref> is a technique for estimating the [[correlation]] between two hypothesised [[normal distribution|normally distributed]] continuous [[latent variable]]s, from two observed [[level of measurement|ordinal variable]]s.  [[Tetrachoric correlation]] is a special case of the polychoric correlation applicable when both observed variables are [[dichotomous variable|dichotomous]].  These names derive from the polychoric and tetrachoric series which are used for estimation of these correlations.

==Applications and examples==
This technique is frequently applied when analysing items on self-report instruments such as [[personality test]]s and [[statistical survey|surveys]] that often use [[rating scale]]s with a small number of response options (e.g., strongly disagree to strongly agree). The smaller the number of response categories, the more a correlation between latent continuous variables will tend to be attenuated.
Lee, Poon & Bentler (1995) have recommended a two-step approach to [[factor analysis]] for assessing the factor structure of tests involving ordinally measured items.<ref name="lee1995">{{Cite journal|last1=Lee|first1=S.-Y.|last2=Poon|first2=W. Y.|last3=Bentler|first3=P. M.|year=1995|title=A two-stage estimation of structural equation models with continuous and polytomous variables|journal=British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology|volume=48|pages=339–358}}</ref> Kiwanuka and colleagues (2022) have also illustrated the application of polychoric correlations and polychoric [[confirmatory factor analysis]] in nursing science.<ref name="kiwanuka2022">{{Cite journal|last1=Kiwanuka|first1=F.|last2=Kopra|first2=J.|last3=Sak-Dankosky|first3=N.|last4=Nanyonga|first4=R. C.|last5=Kvist|first5=T.|year=2022|title=Polychoric Correlation with Ordinal Data in Nursing Research|journal=Nursing Research|doi=10.1097/NNR.0000000000000614|pmc=9617753}}</ref> This aims to reduce the effect of statistical artifacts, such as the number of response scales or [[skewness]] of variables leading to items grouping together in factors. In some disciplines, the statistical technique is rarely applied; however, some scholars have demonstrated how it can be used as an alternative to the Pearson correlation.<ref name="lww">{{Cite journal|title=Polychoric Correlation with Ordinal Data in Nursing Research|journal=Nursing Research|publisher=Lippincott Williams & Wilkins|url=https://journals.lww.com/nursingresearchonline/Abstract/9900/Polychoric_Correlation_with_Ordinal_Data_in.15.aspx}}</ref>

==Software==
* Mplus by Muthen and Muthen [https://www.statmodel.com/]
* polycor package in R by John Fox [https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/polycor/]
* psych package in R by William Revelle [https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/psych/index.html]
* lavaan package in R by Yves Rosseel [https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lavaan/index.html]
* semopy package in Python by Georgy Meshcheryakov [https://semopy.com/]
* PRELIS
* [https://www.john-uebersax.com/stat/xpc.htm POLYCORR program]
* PROC CORR in SAS (with POLYCHORIC or OUTPLC= options) [https://support.sas.com/documentation/cdl/en/procstat/67528/HTML/default/viewer.htm#procstat_corr_syntax01.htm]
* package polychoric in Stata by Stas Kolenikov [https://web.archive.org/web/20160327054012/http://web.missouri.edu/~kolenikovs/stata/]
